purpose: Atovaquone is used to treat and prevent certain parasitic infections, including a type of pneumonia called Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) that can affect people with weakened immune systems. It is also used in combination with another medication to prevent and treat malaria. Your doctor may prescribe it if you are traveling to an area where malaria is common or if your immune system is weakened.
how_it_works: Atovaquone works by blocking a specific energy-producing process that parasites need to survive and grow. Think of it like cutting off the parasite's power supply — without energy, the parasite cannot multiply and eventually dies. Importantly, this process is different in humans, so the medication can target the parasite without harming your own cells.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, headache, rash, fever, and trouble sleeping are the most commonly reported side effects. Some people also notice mild dizziness or feeling unusually tired.
warnings: Take atovaquone with food, ideally a fatty meal, because food greatly improves how well your body absorbs this medication — without food, it may not work as well. Tell your doctor if you have liver or kidney problems, as this may affect how you tolerate it. Let your doctor know about all other medications you take, since some drugs can interact with atovaquone and reduce its effectiveness. If you develop a severe rash or signs of a serious allergic reaction, seek medical attention right away.
typical_dosing: For PCP treatment in adults, the usual dose is 750 mg (about 5 mL of liquid) taken twice daily with food for 21 days. For PCP prevention, it is typically 1500 mg (10 mL) once daily with food. For malaria prevention (as Malarone), the usual adult dose is one tablet daily starting 1-2 days before travel, continuing during travel, and for 7 days after returning. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
